# CHAPTER XI:

THE BATTLE OF THE RAMS (1863)

Minister Adams troubled himself little about what he did not see of an enemy. His son, a nervous animal, made life a terror by seeing too much. Earl Russell suited the Minister; Henry Adams never saw Russell without being amused by his droll likeness to John Quincy Adams. Whether Russell were true or false mattered less, for in either case the Legation could act only as though he were false. Had the Minister known Russell's determined effort to betray and ruin him in October, 1862, he could scarcely have used stronger expressions than he did in 1863. Russell's *idée fixe* was the nullity or fatuity of the Washington Government; but after the failure of his last effort for joint intervention on November 12, 1862, only one week elapsed before he received from Mr. Adams a note repeating his charges about the Alabama and asking in very plain language for redress. Both Palmerston and Russell were senile from youth; they had never got beyond 1815. Russell could not conceive that he had misunderstood and mismanaged Minister Adams from the start, and on the defensive he showed mere confusion and helplessness.

Whatever the theory, the action of diplomacy had to be the same. The Minister was obliged to imply collusion. He could not stop at criminal negligence; no one could be so simple as to believe that two armored ships-of-war could be built publicly, under the eyes of the Government, and go to sea like the Alabama, without active and incessant collusion. The longer Earl Russell kept on his mask of assumed ignorance, the more violently in the end the Minister would have to tear it off.

As the spring of 1863 drew on, the vast field cleared itself for action. After two years of solitude, one began to feel the first faint flush of new and imperial life. One was twenty-five years old, and quite ready to assert it. With an intensity more painful than that of any Shakespearean drama, men's eyes were fastened on the armies in the field. As the huge masses struck, one after another, with the precision of machinery, the opposing mass, the world shivered. During the July days Londoners were stupid with unbelief. They were learning from the Yankees how to fight.

News of Vicksburg and Gettysburg reached London one Sunday afternoon, and that evening Henry Adams was asked to a small reception at the house of Monckton Milnes. He arrived early and found only the ladies in the drawing-room; presently the gentlemen came in, and, as luck would have it, Delane of the *Times* came first. When Milnes caught sight of his young American friend, with a whoop of triumph he rushed to throw both arms about his neck and kiss him on both cheeks. For the first time in his life, Adams happened not to be thinking of himself. He was thinking of Delane, whose eye caught his at the moment of Milnes's embrace. Delane probably regarded it as a piece of Milnes's foolery; he had never heard of young Adams, and never dreamed of his resentment at being ridiculed in the *Times*. The British mind is the slowest of all minds, and the capture of Vicksburg had not yet penetrated Delane's thick cortex of fixed ideas. It needed a whole generation for the *Times* to reach Milnes's standpoint.

For nearly a year the private secretary had watched the board arranging itself for the collision between the Legation and Delane, who stood behind the Palmerston Ministry. The Legation was still as weakly manned as those of Guatemala or Portugal — the Secretary, the Assistant Secretary, and the private secretary did all the work the Minister did not do; a great staff would have suppressed him, and he was rather better off than the rest, because he was invisible and unknown. The Minister had a staff of active consuls, a well-organized press, efficient legal support, and a swarm of social allies permeating all classes. All he needed was a victory in the field, and Secretary Stanton undertook that part of diplomacy. Vicksburg and Gettysburg cleared the board.

In the Legation no great confidence was felt in stopping the rams. Russell seemed immovable. Little by little, Minister Adams lost hope. With loss of hope came the raising of tone, until at last, after stripping Russell of every rag of defence, he closed by leaving him loaded with connivance in the rebel armaments, and ended by the famous sentence: "It would be superfluous in me to point out to your lordship that this is war!"

What the Minister meant by this was his own affair; what the private secretary understood by it was a part of his education. Had his father ordered him to draft an explanatory paragraph to expand the idea, he would have continued thus: —

"It would be superfluous: 1st. Because Earl Russell not only knows it already, but has meant it from the start. 2nd. Because it is the only logical and necessary consequence of his unvarying action. 3d. Because Mr. Adams is not pointing out to him that 'this is war,' but is pointing it out to the world, to complete the record."

The war was Russell's war — Adams only accepted it.

Russell's reply reached the Legation on September 8, announcing at last that "instructions have been issued which will prevent the departure of the two ironclad vessels from Liverpool." The members of the Legation in Portland Place accepted it as Grant had accepted the capitulation of Vicksburg. Though Minister Adams should stay in office till he were ninety, he would never fight another campaign of life and death like this; and though the private secretary should attain every office in the gift of President or people, he would never again find education to compare with this two-year-and-a-half struggle in London. For once, the volunteer secretary was satisfied with his Government. The American Minister had trumped their best card and won the game.

Again and again, in after life, he went back over the ground. He found no error on either side. All the more he was disconcerted that Russell should indignantly, to his dying day, deny and resent the axiom of Adams's whole contention, that from the first he meant to break up the Union. Russell affirmed that he meant nothing of the sort; that he meant nothing at all; that he meant to do right; that he did not know what he meant. Driven from one defence after another, he pleaded at last, like Gladstone, that he had no defence. What was worse for the private secretary, to the total derision and despair of the lifelong effort for education — he proved it.

When the biography in 1889 published papers that upset all Henry Adams had taken for diplomatic education, he sat down once more, past sixty, to see whether he could unravel the skein. Russell proved that he had been feeble, timid, mistaken, senile, but not dishonest. The Lairds had built their ships in reliance on the known opinion of the law-officers that the statute did not apply, and a jury would not convict. Tacitly Russell connived with Laird; he allowed the builders to go on till the ships were ready for sea. Then, on September 3, two days before Mr. Adams's "superfluous" letter, he wrote to Lord Palmerston: "The conduct of the gentlemen who have contracted for the two ironclads at Birkenhead is so very suspicious," — calling "suspicious" what no one else in Europe or America felt any suspicion about — "that I have thought it necessary to direct that they should be detained."

For *naïveté* that would be unusual in an unpaid *attaché* of Legation, this sudden leap from his own to his opponent's ground, after two years and a half of dogged resistance, might have roused Palmerston to inhuman scorn; but Palmerston met the appeal with wonderful loyalty, finding that there was no lawful ground for meddling with the ironclads, and suggesting that they be bought for the British Navy. Russell, by this time, was floundering in other troubles: he had neglected to notify the American Minister. His note, saying merely that the matter was under "serious and anxious consideration," did not reach the Legation till three o'clock on the afternoon of September 5 — after the "superfluous" declaration of war had been sent. Thus, Lord Russell had sacrificed the Lairds; cost his Ministry the price of two ironclads, besides the Alabama Claims; and put himself in the position of appearing to yield only to a threat of war. Finally he wrote to the Admiralty a letter which would have sounded youthful from an Eton schoolboy: —

> September 14, 1863.
> MY DEAR DUKE: —
>
> It is of the utmost importance and urgency that the ironclads building at Birkenhead should not go to America to break the blockade. They belong to Monsieur Bravay of Paris. If you will offer to buy them on the part of the Admiralty you will get money's worth if he accepts your offer; and if he does not, it will be presumptive proof that they are already bought by the Confederates. I should state that we have suggested to the Turkish Government to buy them; but you can easily settle that matter with the Turks....

The hilarity of the secretaries in Portland Place would have been loud had they seen this letter; but these papers upset from top to bottom the results of the private secretary's diplomatic education forty years after he had supposed it complete.

To reconstruct, past sixty, an education useful for any practical purpose, is no practical problem. He no longer cared whether he understood human nature or not; he understood quite as much of it as he wanted. But he found in the *Life of Gladstone* a remark that gave him matter for curious thought. "I always hold," said Mr. Gladstone, "that politicians are the men whom, as a rule, it is most difficult to comprehend"; and he added: "For my own part, I never have thus understood, or thought I understood, above one or two."

Earl Russell was certainly not one of the two.

Henry Adams thought he also had understood one or two; but the American type was more familiar. Perhaps this was the sufficient result of his diplomatic education; it seemed to be the whole.
